60-017.r: Kerala → largest rubber producer in India (2024-25). Wrong pairs in the options: UP–Jute, Assam–Wheat, Gujarat–Tea.

60-018.r: Stimulant crops: tea, coffee, tobacco, opium poppy, datura, hemp, betel nut. Wheat → Rabi crop; maize and tur (arhar) → Kharif crops.

60-019.r: Tea Board: statutory body (section 4, Tea Act 1953; constituted 1954), under Ministry of Commerce, HQ Kolkata; overseas offices Dubai and Moscow when asked → statements 1 and 4.
60-019.t: Tea Board comes under the Commerce Ministry, not the Agriculture Ministry; its HQ is Kolkata, not Bengaluru.

61-001.r: Karnataka (also Tamil Nadu) grows all three: coffee, rubber and tobacco.

61-002.r: Plantation crops: tea, coffee, rubber (Ministry of Commerce) + coconut, arecanut, palm, cocoa, cashew (Ministry of Agriculture). Answer set: tea, rubber, coconut, coffee.

61-003.r: Tea → main crop of Assam; tobacco → large scale in Andhra Pradesh (now Gujarat leads). Coffee leader is Karnataka, not Tamil Nadu; Chhattisgarh's main crop is paddy, not jute.

61-004.r: Tobacco (2024-25): Gujarat leads with 45.23% of production; Andhra Pradesh second (30.22%). When asked, Andhra Pradesh gave over one-third.

61-005.r: Largest tobacco producers (2024-25): Gujarat > Andhra Pradesh > Uttar Pradesh > Karnataka. Among the options when asked, Uttar Pradesh was largest.

61-007.r: Area under tobacco (2024-25): Gujarat 204.79 thousand ha > Andhra Pradesh 139 > Karnataka 79 > Uttar Pradesh 33.29. In 2010, Andhra Pradesh had the largest area.
61-007.c: The book prints (d) Gujarat, the 2024-25 leader; for 2010, the year asked, its own explanation names Andhra Pradesh.

61-008.r: Coconut: Kerala was top when asked; now (2024-25, 3rd A.E.) Tamil Nadu 1st, Kerala 2nd, Karnataka 3rd.

61-009.r: Coconut share (2024-25, 3rd AE): Tamil Nadu 30.17% > Kerala 27.08% > Karnataka 24.95%. Kerala was the answer when asked.

61-010.r: India led black pepper and ginger (when asked), so no code fits; cardamom leader Guatemala, cloves Indonesia. 2022: India 2nd in black pepper after Vietnam.

61-011.r: Odisha is not known for cardamom. Leading small-cardamom producers (2024-25): Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka.

61-012.r: Kerala → world-famous for spices since ancient times.

61-013.r: Kerala → 'Garden of Spices' / 'Spice Garden' of India. But the largest spice producer (2024-25, 3rd A.E.) is Madhya Pradesh.
61-013.t: Don't confuse: Kerala is the 'garden of spices'; Madhya Pradesh is the top spice producer.

61-015.r: Small cardamom → Kerala largest (2024-25). Black pepper → Karnataka 1st, Kerala 2nd; Karnataka is not in the options, so Kerala.

61-016.r: Clove → flower-bud of a medium-sized evergreen plant (Eugenia caryophyllata); a spice also used in medicines.

61-017.r: Cloves are farmed (2024-25) in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, so three options fit; the book calls the question wrong and gives no single answer (*).

61-018.r: Black pepper climate: hot and moist, at least 200 cm annual rain, slopes 1100–1300 m high, annual temperature 15°C–30°C.

61-020.r: Largest spice producer: Gujarat when asked; now (2024-25, 3rd AE) Madhya Pradesh.

61-021.r: Cashew nut top producers (2024-25): Maharashtra > Andhra Pradesh > Odisha.

61-022.r: Saffron → Jammu and Kashmir, the only producer among the options (UT since 31 October 2019); grown there since ancient times.

61-023.r: Wrong pair: Rubber–Himachal Pradesh; Kerala is the largest rubber producer. Correct: Jute–West Bengal, Tea–Assam, Sugarcane–Uttar Pradesh.

62-001.r: Jhuming (Paida) → shifting cultivation by tribes: cut the jungle, leave it to dry, then farm; shift to a new place when fertility falls.

62-004.r: Jhum → mostly in north-eastern hills: Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya; also practised by tribals in Assam's hills.

62-005.r: Slash-and-burn (Jhum) → north-eastern states (Arunachal, Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, Sikkim; 'Pamlou' in Manipur). Farmers shift when soil fertility drops; low productivity, no fertiliser.

62-006.r: Jhum problem in hilly areas: Assam and Bihar when asked; the book says today's answer would be Odisha and Madhya Pradesh.

62-007.r: Shifting cultivation names: Western Ghats → Kumari; south-east Rajasthan → Waltre; north-east India → Jhum; Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh → Dahiya.

62-008.r: Wrong pair: Mashan–Himachal Pradesh; Mashan is in Madhya Pradesh. Correct: Pondu–Odisha, Poonam–Kerala, Jhoom–Assam.

63-001.r: Seed tags: Breeder seed → golden; Foundation seed → white; Certified seed (made from foundation seed) → blue.
63-001.h: Seed chain Breeder → Foundation → Certified = Golden → White → Blue.

63-002.r: Area 1980-81 to 2024-25 (million ha): wheat 22.28→32.80, rice 40.15→51.27, pulses 22.46→27.72 rose; coarse cereals 41.78→25.75 fell, with fluctuations → 'None of these'.

63-003.r: When asked: Kerala–Tapioca, West Bengal–Flax, Gujarat–Groundnut correct. Top producers 2024-25: Tapioca–Tamil Nadu, Cotton–Maharashtra, Jute & Mesta–West Bengal, Groundnut–Gujarat.

63-004.r: Banana–Maharashtra was the wrong pair when asked. Now top producers: Potato–Uttar Pradesh (also in 2013), Coconut–Tamil Nadu, Banana–Maharashtra (2023-24), Tobacco–Gujarat.

63-006.r: National Research Centre for Banana (NRCB) → Tiruchirappalli (Trichy), Tamil Nadu; set up 21 August 1993.

63-007.r: Map question: area 4 (Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, part of Maharashtra) marks the non-cereal crop area; areas 1–3 are cereal areas.

63-008.r: Foodgrain output 2024-25 (final): Rice 150.2 > Wheat 117.9 > Coarse grain 63.9 > Pulses 25.7 million tonnes.

63-009.r: Largest foodgrain producer (2024-25 final): Uttar Pradesh 17.85%; then Madhya Pradesh 13.04%, Punjab 9.16%.

63-010.r: Gujarat led cotton, groundnut, salt and milk when asked. Now Gujarat leads groundnut and salt (2024-25); Uttar Pradesh leads milk (2023-24).

63-011.r: When asked: Cotton–Gujarat, Gram–Madhya Pradesh, Black pepper–Kerala, Pineapple–West Bengal. Now: Cotton and Gram–Maharashtra (2024-25), Black pepper–Karnataka, Pineapple–West Bengal (2023-24).

63-012.r: Most grown: Ragi → Karnataka; Bajra → Rajasthan; Jowar → Maharashtra; Urad → Madhya Pradesh.

63-013.r: Wrong pair: Potato–Madhya Pradesh; Uttar Pradesh is the top potato producer (2024-25). Coffee–Karnataka, Wheat–Uttar Pradesh correct; cotton now led by Maharashtra.

63-014.r: Crop pests: Rice → Ghundi bug; Wheat → Aphid; Sugarcane → Top shoot borer moth; Gram → Bollworm.

63-015.r: Crop diseases: Sugarcane → Red rot; Paddy → Khaira; Arhar → Wilt; Potato → Late blight.

63-016.r: Wrong pair: Rice–Green hair; green hair disease is found in millet. Correct: Bajra–Ergot, Pea–Powdery mildew, Gram–Wilt.

63-017.r: Sugarcane, beetroot, sweet pea, gram, arhar and French bean belong to three plant families.

63-018.r: India is not the largest producer of any option (FAO 2024): 2nd in sugarcane, 7th in green coffee, 2nd in unmanufactured tobacco. The book gives no single answer (*).

63-019.r: Foodgrain production 2011-12: 259.29 million tonnes (final estimate), matching no option; CGPSC deleted the question. 2024-25 estimate: 357.7 million tonnes.

63-020.r: FAO 2024: India 1st in fruit production (other fruits n.e.c.) and 2nd largest exporter of unmanufactured tobacco. When asked, both statements were false (d).

63-021.r: Jute → Kharif crop (not Rabi); needs high temperature (24°C–35°C), heavy rain (125–200 cm), low plains; grown mainly in eastern India (West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha).

63-022.r: Jute is indigenous to India (A true). Kharif crop, sown February–June, harvested July–October (R true), but R doesn't explain A. White jute: primary origin Africa, secondary India–Myanmar region.

63-023.r: India → world's largest producer of raw jute and jute goods (National Jute Board): A true. Yellow Revolution = oilseeds, not jute: R false.
63-023.t: Yellow Revolution is about oilseeds, not jute.

63-024.r: Largest Jute & Mesta producer (2024-25): West Bengal, followed by Bihar and Assam.

63-025.r: Jute industry → mainly West Bengal, the major jute & mesta producer (2024-25). Jute grows in loamy soil.

63-026.r: Lower Gangetic plain (humid, hot all year) → best suited to paddy and jute.

63-027.r: Area under jute & mesta (2024-25): West Bengal 0.43 million ha (largest); Bihar 0.06; Assam 0.06.

63-028.r: Fibre crops: cotton, jute, sunhemp (also flax). Top producers (2024-25): cotton → Maharashtra; jute & mesta → West Bengal.

63-029.r: Maize (corn) → can be grown throughout the year; versatile, widely adapted; called 'Queen of Cereals' globally.

63-031.r: Maize uses: starch (dextrin etc.), oil as biodiesel feedstock, alcoholic drinks (corn whisky) → all three statements correct.

63-032.r: Maize matures in about 90–150 days (varies by climatic zone; winter varieties take longer) → answer 110 days.

63-033.r: Maize → C4 plant. Rice, wheat, barley, rye, soybean, cotton, tobacco, potato → C3 plants.
63-033.t: Don't confuse: maize is C4, while rice and wheat are C3.

63-034.r: Maize order when asked: Andhra Pradesh > Karnataka > Rajasthan > Bihar. 2024-25 top three: Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Bihar.

63-035.r: Shaktiman-I and Shaktiman-II → varieties of maize (the book calls them genetically modified).
63-035.c: The book calls them genetically modified; Shaktiman-I and II are quality protein maize (QPM) hybrids from conventional breeding, not GM crops.

63-036.r: Commercial saffron (Zaffran) → Jammu and Kashmir (then a state, now a UT).

63-037.r: Most saffron in India → Kashmir valley. Other world producers: Spain, Iran, Greece, Italy.

63-038.r: Barley → cool climate, poorer soil; Rice → hot, moist, rich soil; Millets → hot, dry, poor soil; Tea → warm, moist, high altitude.

63-039.h: Jute is the wettest and hottest (1500–2000 mm, 25–35°C); flax the coolest (5–18°C).

63-040.r: Onion → seeds sown first, young plants then transplanted (grown by transplanting seedlings).

63-041.r: Best crop cycle for eastern Uttar Pradesh: Paddy – Maize – Wheat.

63-042.r: Frederick Wilson → started Rajma and potato cultivation in Bhagirathi valley; first white man to settle there (19th century); called 'Pahari' and 'Raja of Harsil'.

63-043.r: Board HQs: Coffee Board → Bengaluru; Rubber Board → Kottayam; Tea Board → Kolkata; Tobacco Board → Guntur.
63-043.h: HQ near the crop: coffee in Karnataka (Bengaluru), rubber in Kerala (Kottayam), tobacco in Andhra (Guntur).

63-044.r: Vegetables: India 2nd in the world after China (FAO 2024, other vegetables fresh n.e.c.).

63-046.r: Sindhu → seedless mango variety developed by Indian scientists; the only seedless mango variety in the world.

63-047.r: Amrapali mango = hybrid of Dasheri × Neelam, developed in 1971 by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (Pusa), Delhi.

63-048.r: Lalit → improved guava variety from the horticulture research institute at Lucknow; recommended for commercial production.

63-049.r: Regular-bearing mango varieties: Dasheri-51, Bangalora (Totapuri), Neelam, Amrapali. Dasheri-1, Chausa and Langra are not → 'None of the above'.

63-050.r: Kanchan, Krishna and Banarasi → improved varieties of Indian gooseberry (Amla), rich in Vitamin C.

63-051.r: No known variety is called 'Ganga Varanasi'. Kashi Ganga → bottle gourd; Kashi Madhu → muskmelon; Banarasi → aonla (and guava). The book gives no single answer (*).

63-052.r: Wrong pair: Wheat–Shusk Samrat; Shusk Samrat is a rice variety. Correct: Paddy–Govind, Arhar–Paras, Pea–Prakash.

63-053.r: Banana: Tamil Nadu top when asked; now (2023-24) Maharashtra > Andhra Pradesh > Tamil Nadu.

63-054.r: Bajra: Gujarat was a leading producer when asked; top three now (2024-25): Rajasthan > Uttar Pradesh > Haryana.
